title: Memory Hazard Index: adaptive budgeting & soft-preemption for weights/KV/activations
creator: Asha Patel
description: Introduce a Memory Hazard Index (MHI) and 'soft-preempt' orchestration that dynamically budgets GPU memory across weights, KV cache, and activations for continuous-batching inference. The MHI is a single scalar per-GPU derived from current KV occupancy, active weight residency, predicted activation tail from ongoing batched requests, and a short-term entropy of incoming sequence-length distribution. The goal is to reduce abrupt OOMs and minimize conservative static headroom reserves by enabling anticipatory, graded preemption and ephemeral compression steps (e.g., KV eviction, activation compression, lightweight offload) before hard failures.
acceptance_criteria: MHI computed every 50ms in the serving runtime for GPU pools in staging
Soft-preempt policy triggers graded actions (evict-KV->compress-activations->spill-to-host) with decreasing disruption tiers
Simulated stressbench shows >= 80% reduction in hard OOM events vs baseline and <= 10% tail-latency regressions for P95
Integration tests for continuous-batching paths exercise at least 3 preempt tiers and validate KV integrity post-eviction
Dashboard exposes per-GPU MHI, last-triggered action, and predicted headroom margin for operator debugging
notes: Design trade-offs: centralized controller vs per-GPU local MHI. We propose hybrid: per-GPU local MHI with opportunistic peer gossip for cross-GPU rebalancing to keep reaction latency <100ms.
KV eviction strategy should prefer LRU windows per-tenant and maintain a minimum pinned prefix for in-flight requests to avoid correctness regressions.

Activation compression candidate is a lossy quantized snapshot only used transiently during spill windows; must be reversible before response finalization or trigger graceful fallback to smaller model variant.
We must instrument the runtime to capture accurate sequence-length forecasts over a 1s horizon to feed the MHI entropy term. Use EMA with 200ms half-life for responsiveness.
